sws_p2c4: How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better. I think a fear that keeps turning up to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you. If it sounds like your little one, though, hear it out the first time it shows up. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you're in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it's your little one asking.
sws_p3b3: I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder. That part learns it has to shout when nobody listens, or when the inherited critic voice makes fun of it.
sws_p5ab2: Even then, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and what it has you doing instead. Maybe the laundry suddenly feels urgent, and the reaction has stopped you from looking for your little one. Whether that's what the reaction is trying to stop is only a guess, and it might not be protecting you at all.
sws_p5ac: You'd be guessing whether the reaction is protecting you, and from what. What it ends up keeping you from might be something else. You can still watch that, and what sets the reaction off. Maybe the laundry suddenly feels urgent right as you start looking for your little one, and once you're up, you don't sit back down.
sws_p5bc2: Or you might get an answer, as a voice or just a hunch. If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything you can't take back can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what's actually happened (if you're in danger, get safe first). Those checks are only for advice, though, and if it's grief or anger, you'd listen either way.
